plan.topic: Lab-acquired plague in the US: the fatal 2009 Chicago case of a researcher infected with a weakened (attenuated) Yersinia pestis strain who had undiagnosed hereditary hemochromatosis (CDC MMWR, Feb 25, 2011)
plan.angle: A calm, well-documented case study built only on the CDC MMWR report (and the CDC Stacks record). At most one neutral line of news context ('plague has been in the news this month'), with no claims about the Irkutsk case. Don't lead with the researcher's name. Segments: (1) What an attenuated strain is and why this one was considered lower-risk (it lacks the pigmentation locus, so it depends on iron). (2) The timeline and clinical course in MMWR's wording. (3) How the investigation found hereditary hemochromatosis (iron overload) and why it's thought to have let the weakened strain cause severe infection. Use MMWR's hedged verbs such as 'might have' or 'likely'. (4) CDC's conclusion: likely an unrecognized occupational exposure, with no clear route identified. Keep MMWR's exact scope. (5) Contact follow-up and preventive antibiotics as MMWR reports them; no secondary cases. (6) What MMWR recommended for labs: awareness, reporting exposures and illness, and medical follow-up. Mention BMBL practices (updated Mar 18, 2026) only in that source's own words. (7) What it means for the public: plague 'can be cured with antibiotics, especially when started early' (CDC). Close: possible exposure plus fever, cough, shortness of breath or chest pain means contact a doctor or local health authority urgently. Then 'If you're worried, talk to a health professional.' Visuals: lab scene, iron-in-blood diagram, timeline cards. No patient imagery, skulls or rats.
plan.working_title: Plague in a US Lab: What CDC Learned From a 2009 Chicago Case
plan.why: A deep primary source (CDC MMWR) that can be checked line by line. Interest is new (Céline Gounder's Oct 10 comparison), competition is low, and the body doesn't depend on unresolved news, which is what keeps holding plague long videos.

script.working_title: Plague in a Chicago Lab: What CDC Learned From a 2009 Case

scenes.narration: In 2009, a researcher in Chicago died from a plague strain that had been weakened on purpose, and that wasn't known to have caused any lab infection before.
CDC investigated and published the whole thing in its Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report on Feb 25, 2011. And the explanation wasn't only in the bacterium.
Part of it sat in an inherited condition that investigators found no evidence he knew about. It's often silent for years, and it was only identified after his death.
By the end of this you'll know what the word attenuated actually means, what CDC thinks may have undone it, and why no additional infections were found in anyone else.

items: Why no one else got sick

scenes.narration: Plague has been in the news this month. This video isn't about that. Every fact here comes from CDC, WHO and NIH sources.

visual.fact: No claims about any current case

scenes.section: A strain that can't get iron
scenes.narration: Start with the strain. Because the safety in this story was supposed to come partly from the bacterium itself.

scenes.section: A strain that can't get iron
scenes.narration: Plague is caused by a bacterium called Yersinia pestis. It still circulates in rodents and their fleas on several continents, and it causes three forms of illness: bubonic, septicemic and pneumonic.

scenes.section: A strain that can't get iron
scenes.narration: Laboratories study it for a reason. You cannot build better vaccines, faster tests or better treatments for a bacterium you refuse to grow.

scenes.section: A strain that can't get iron
scenes.narration: To make that work safer, researchers use attenuated strains. Weakened versions of the bacterium, widely used in research, and this one wasn't known to have caused lab infections or human deaths.

visual.myth: Lab strains are the same as wild plague
visual.fact: CDC: attenuated, widely used, not known to have caused lab infections

scenes.section: A strain that can't get iron
scenes.narration: The strain in this story was missing a stretch of DNA that microbiologists call the pigmentation locus.

scenes.section: A strain that can't get iron
scenes.narration: Inside that stretch sit genes the bacterium uses to pull iron out of its host. Lose them, and it loses its grocery run.

scenes.section: A strain that can't get iron
scenes.narration: Because iron, strange as it sounds, is at the center of this story.
scenes.on_screen_text: It keeps coming back to iron

visual.fact: Iron is central to this story

scenes.retention_device: Short punch line setting up the key idea

scenes.section: A strain that can't get iron
scenes.narration: In your body, iron isn't lying around loose. It's locked up inside proteins, which means bacteria that need it have to fight for every atom.

visual.stock_query: cartoon iron atoms inside safe vault
visual.fact: Iron is tightly bound in the body

scenes.section: A strain that can't get iron
scenes.narration: Wild plague comes equipped for that fight. This strain did not. In CDC's mouse tests, both the patient's strain and its parent strain killed fewer than 3% of mice, even at doses as high as 100 million bacteria.

visual.stat_label: CDC mouse tests, up to 100 million bacteria

scenes.retention_device: Hard number instead of an absolute

scenes.section: A strain that can't get iron
scenes.narration: With one exception. CDC's report notes that in animal studies, injecting iron at the same time can make these strains more virulent.
scenes.retention_device: The hinge of the whole video

scenes.section: A strain that can't get iron
scenes.narration: Hold on to that word. Iron. It comes back, and it changes everything.

scenes.section: A strain that can't get iron
scenes.narration: That's precisely why strains like this get chosen in the first place. Lower risk to the people doing the work.
scenes.retention_device: Resolves why anyone would use it

scenes.narration: Now the timeline, in the terms the report uses.
In September 2009, the researcher developed fever, body aches and a cough.
Nothing about that points to plague. It points to a respiratory virus. In fact, the clinic he first visited suspected influenza or another acute respiratory infection, according to CDC's report.

visual.fact: CDC: the clinic suspected flu or another respiratory infection

scenes.narration: Several days later he was taken to a hospital, severely ill. He died soon after.
Blood samples had been taken at the hospital. After his death, those cultures grew a bacterium.
Further testing identified it as Yersinia pestis, and matched it to the attenuated strain used in his own laboratory.
scenes.on_screen_text: Matched to his own lab strain
scenes.retention_device: Payoff with a bigger question attached

scenes.narration: Sit with that for a second. A strain that kills fewer than 3% of mice in the lab had been multiplying in a person's bloodstream.
And plague was only identified after he died. CDC's report describes the cause as likely an unrecognized occupational exposure. That's the first lesson of this case.

visual.fact: CDC: likely an unrecognized occupational exposure

scenes.narration: So the investigation had two questions. How did it get into him? And why did it do this?
Investigators pulled on every thread they could find.
They reviewed his laboratory work, his equipment and his procedures. They reviewed his medical history. And there was an autopsy.

The autopsy findings were consistent with septicemic plague, infection in the blood, and inconsistent with pneumonic plague. It found no signs of pneumonia, bowel perforation or endocarditis. But it did find something else.
His tissues showed iron overload.

visual.stock_query: cartoon liver glowing with iron dots

scenes.narration: Genetic testing found he was homozygous for the C282Y variant in a gene called HFE. That variant is the one most often behind hereditary hemochromatosis.
The diagnosis was made only after his death. Investigators found no evidence he knew he had it.
Hereditary hemochromatosis is an inherited condition in which the body absorbs too much iron from food and stores the excess in organs such as the liver and heart.
scenes.on_screen_text: The body stores too much iron

visual.fact: NIH: excess iron builds up in organs

scenes.narration: NIH says about 1 in 15 people of Northern European ancestry carry at least one copy of that variant. It's much less common in people of Asian or African ancestry. And many people have no symptoms for years.

visual.stat_label: NIH: Northern European ancestry, at least one C282Y copy

scenes.narration: It's also treatable. NIH describes removing blood on a schedule as the main treatment, because taking out blood takes iron with it.

visual.fact: NIH: blood removal is the main treatment

scenes.narration: Now put the two halves of this story side by side.
The strain was weakened for one specific reason. It struggled to get iron.
And the person it ended up in had iron overload. Postmortem tests found his serum iron was more than three times the top of the reference range.
scenes.on_screen_text: Serum iron: 3x+ the top of normal (postmortem)

visual.stat_label: Postmortem serum iron vs top of reference range

scenes.narration: The report also notes he had insulin-dependent diabetes. CDC points out that diabetes is a known risk factor for more severe bacterial infections. It doesn't say diabetes explains this case. If you live with diabetes and have questions about infection risk, talk to your clinician.

visual.fact: CDC: diabetes is a known risk factor for more severe bacterial infections

scenes.retention_device: Completes the host picture for an audience that often lives with diabetes

scenes.narration: CDC's report is careful here, so I will be too. It calls this one possible explanation: that his iron overload might have given the strain enough iron to overcome its defect and become virulent.

visual.myth: The iron condition caused his death

scenes.narration: Might have. Not proved. One case, one report, with the hedges left in on purpose.
But the idea is hard to shake. Because this strain's weakness was never a property of the bacterium alone.
Think of a lock that only works because the room is dark. The lock is real. Turn the lights on, and it stops mattering.
scenes.on_screen_text: A lock that needs the dark

scenes.narration: On CDC's reading, the attenuation was a dependency. It leaned on the host keeping iron scarce. In a body with iron to spare, that dependency may loosen.

visual.fact: Scarce iron was the safety condition

scenes.narration: One thing this does not say. It doesn't tell us how wild plague behaves in people with hemochromatosis. That isn't what this report studied. If you have hemochromatosis or questions about your iron levels, that's a conversation for your clinician.

visual.fact: Scope: one attenuated strain, one case

scenes.narration: And here's where the report gets blunt. CDC's investigation found gaps in biosafety practice, including inconsistent use of gloves, which it says could have allowed the bacteria in through the skin. It doesn't say that's definitely what happened.

visual.myth: Nothing about the practices was off
visual.fact: CDC: inconsistent glove use could have allowed skin exposure

scenes.narration: The report also notes poor attendance at required biosafety training. Which brings us to the part that still unsettles people who read it.

visual.fact: CDC noted poor biosafety training attendance

scenes.retention_device: New open loop before chapter change

scenes.narration: How did the bacterium get into him?
CDC's conclusion was that the cause of death likely was an unrecognized occupational exposure. The strain came from his own laboratory, so the source itself was never in doubt.

visual.fact: CDC: likely an unrecognized occupational exposure

scenes.narration: The route was never pinned down. CDC lists it as unknown. But the autopsy found septicemic plague, infection in the blood, and no evidence of pneumonic plague. CDC says that points to entry through the skin or a mucous membrane, not the lungs.

visual.fact: CDC: suggests a transdermal or mucosal route

scenes.retention_device: Surprising non-answer with a real clue

scenes.narration: That's unsatisfying. It's also the honest finding, and CDC published it that way rather than tidying it up.
And it carries the practical lesson of the whole case. If an exposure can go unnoticed, safety can't depend on people noticing.
scenes.retention_device: Turns the gap into a takeaway

scenes.narration: It has to depend on the routine. Protective equipment used every time, and illness reported early.

visual.stock_query: cartoon worker gloves and report form

scenes.narration: Which raises the question people asked immediately in 2009. Was anyone else in danger?

scenes.section: Why no one else got sick
scenes.narration: Here's the part that should reassure you.

scenes.section: Why no one else got sick
scenes.narration: Investigators identified 30 co-workers, one household contact, and 64 other close contacts, including medical, laboratory and pathology staff.

scenes.section: Why no one else got sick
scenes.narration: Contacts were offered preventive antibiotics. All 30 co-workers were prescribed them, and 61 of the 65 household and other close contacts, 94%, accepted a 7-day course.

visual.stat_label: Household and other close contacts who accepted prophylaxis

scenes.section: Why no one else got sick
scenes.narration: And CDC's words: no additional Yersinia pestis infections have been identified.

scenes.section: Why no one else got sick
scenes.narration: That isn't just luck. His infection was septicemic, not pneumonic. And it's the pneumonic form, in the lungs, that can pass from person to person.

visual.stock_query: cartoon lungs icon and blood drop
visual.myth: Every plague case spreads between people
visual.fact: His infection was septicemic, not the pneumonic form that spreads between people

scenes.section: Why no one else got sick
scenes.narration: WHO's fact sheet is specific. Human-to-human transmission of bubonic plague is rare. The pneumonic form is different: any person with pneumonic plague may transmit the disease via respiratory particles to other humans.
scenes.on_screen_text: WHO: bubonic rarely spreads person to person

visual.quote: Human-to-human transmission of bubonic plague is rare.
visual.attribution: WHO plague fact sheet, updated Sep 29, 2026

scenes.section: Why no one else got sick
scenes.narration: And the response you just heard, tracing contacts and offering preventive antibiotics, is the same playbook that stops plague outbreaks elsewhere.
scenes.retention_device: Connects the case to broader practice

scenes.section: Why no one else got sick
scenes.narration: WHO describes seven-day chemoprophylaxis, meaning preventive antibiotics, for people who have had close contact. That's a decision health authorities make, with a prescription. Never something to arrange yourself.

scenes.section: Why no one else got sick
scenes.narration: So what did CDC actually recommend?
The recommendations are short, and none of them is exotic.

Researchers working with attenuated Yersinia pestis and other potentially infectious material should always use at least Biosafety Level 2 practices. And researchers should always follow recommended use of protective equipment.

visual.fact: CDC: at least BSL-2 practices, plus recommended PPE

scenes.narration: Unexpected illness in a laboratory worker should be reported to the institution. And clinicians should routinely ask patients about their work exposures.
And institutional safety committees should implement and maintain effective surveillance programs to identify and monitor acute illness among laboratory workers.

visual.fact: CDC: surveillance programs to identify and monitor acute illness

scenes.narration: The containment side has its own reference book: Biosafety in Microbiological and Biomedical Laboratories, known as BMBL, updated Mar 18, 2026.
BMBL recommends Biosafety Level 2 practices, equipment and facilities for handling potentially infectious clinical materials and cultures of Yersinia pestis.

visual.fact: BMBL: BSL-2 for potentially infectious materials and cultures

scenes.narration: And it recommends Biosafety Level 3 practices and containment equipment for activities with a high potential for droplet or aerosol production.

visual.fact: BMBL: BSL-3 where aerosol potential is high

scenes.narration: Those tiers exist because risk is never the bacterium alone. It's the bacterium, plus the procedure, plus the person.
And that's the human thing about this case. Two things lined up: everyday gaps in protective practice, and host factors, including a condition nobody had diagnosed.

items: Host factors, incl. an undiagnosed condition

scenes.retention_device: Emotional resonance before the practical turn

scenes.narration: If you don't work in a plague laboratory, here's how to hold this story.
scenes.retention_device: Chapter break addressed to the viewer

scenes.narration: This was an occupational exposure in a research laboratory. It is not how people ordinarily encounter plague.

visual.myth: This is how people usually catch plague

scenes.narration: Naturally occurring plague does still happen. CDC says an average of five human plague cases are reported each year in the United States, with a range of 0 to 17.

visual.stat_label: CDC: average US human cases reported yearly

scenes.narration: The part that matters most is the part CDC states flatly. Plague can be cured with antibiotics, but treatment must be given quickly.

visual.quote: Plague can be cured with antibiotics, but treatment must be given quickly.

scenes.narration: Quickly is the operative word. Which is why the symptoms are worth knowing before you ever need them.
For pneumonic plague, CDC lists fever, headache and weakness, with a fast-developing pneumonia: shortness of breath, chest pain and cough.

items: Fast-developing pneumonia: shortness of breath, chest pain, cough

scenes.narration: More broadly, CDC describes bubonic plague as fever, headache, chills and weakness, with one or more swollen, painful lymph nodes.

If you have a possible exposure plus any of those symptoms, including fever, cough, shortness of breath, chest pain or swollen, painful lymph nodes, contact a doctor or local health authority urgently.
scenes.on_screen_text: CONTACT A DOCTOR OR LOCAL HEALTH AUTHORITY URGENTLY

visual.fact: Possible exposure plus symptoms: act urgently

scenes.narration: And say the thing this 2009 case turned on. Tell them about the possible exposure. CDC's own recommendation is that clinicians ask about work exposures, so the list of possible diagnoses can be widened to include infections picked up at work.

visual.fact: CDC: clinicians should ask about work exposures

scenes.retention_device: Loops the case back to the viewer

scenes.narration: What this is not is a reason to stash antibiotics in a drawer. Preventive antibiotics for contacts are arranged by health authorities, for people they've assessed.
So here's the whole case, compressed into things you can actually carry.

Attenuated doesn't mean zero risk. Host factors may change the math. Protective practices matter even with weakened strains. Occupational exposure belongs in the conversation with your clinician. And plague can be cured with antibiotics, especially when treatment starts quickly.

items: Use PPE even with weak strains

scenes.narration: One case, from 2009, documented in detail. And it's still one of the clearest lessons in how lab risk works.
scenes.retention_device: Elevates the stakes of the lesson

scenes.narration: So here's where the opening puzzle lands. One possible explanation CDC raises is that the weakened strain needed one condition to stay weak, scarce iron, and in this one person that condition may not have been there. Might. Not proved.
scenes.retention_device: Main open loop paid off, honestly

scenes.narration: If you want the rest of this explained just as calmly, how pneumonic plague actually spreads, what lab tests can and can't confirm, and the myths worth dropping, subscribe. That's what we're publishing next.
scenes.retention_device: CTA tied to a specific next benefit

scenes.narration: And if you're worried, talk to a health professional.

sources.title: Fatal Laboratory-Acquired Infection with an Attenuated Yersinia pestis Strain — Chicago, Illinois, 2009
Biosafety in Microbiological and Biomedical Laboratories (BMBL), 6th Edition

factcheck.summary:
I checked the script against the CDC report (MMWR 60(07):201-205, Feb 25, 2011) and against each cited CDC, WHO, NIDDK and BMBL page. Almost everything holds up. Confirmed in the report: the clinic visit for fever, body aches and cough, where influenza or another acute respiratory infection was suspected; the trip to hospital by ambulance on Sept 13 and death the same day; blood cultures turning positive on Sept 14; plague identified after death; autopsy findings consistent with septicemic and inconsistent with pneumonic plague; homozygous HFE C282Y; postmortem serum iron of 541 mcg/dL against a reference range of 40-160 (3.4 times the upper limit); fewer than 3% of mice dying at doses up to 10^8; the 'conceivably… might have' explanation; inconsistent glove use that 'could have resulted in inadvertent transdermal exposure'; 30 co-workers, plus 1 household contact and 64 other close contacts, of whom 61 (94%) accepted prophylaxis; and 'No additional Y. pestis infections have been identified'. The recommendations to use at least BSL-2 practices, follow PPE guidance and run surveillance programs are also confirmed.
Also confirmed: CDC says 'an average of five', range 0-17 (page updated Oct 7, 2026); CDC's exact cure sentence (About Plague, updated Aug 24, 2026); CDC's symptom lists (updated May 15, 2024); WHO's transmission quotes and seven-day prophylaxis (updated Sep 29, 2026); and NIDDK's 1 in 15 figure and its treatment by regularly drawing blood (phlebotomy).
Four issues need fixing. (1) The hook and scene s09 say the strain was 'weakened on purpose'. The report only says the strain is 'attenuated as a result of defects in its ability to acquire iron'. It doesn't say the weakening was deliberate, and the pgm deletion is normally spontaneous. (2) Scene s30 says 'tissues' showed iron overload, but the report found iron deposits in the liver only, not in the pancreas or heart. (3) Scenes s65 and s80 slightly merge two separate CDC recommendations. (4) A few small wording mismatches. The safety and urgency lines and the diabetes and hemochromatosis caveats are all good.

issues.claim: a plague strain that had been weakened on purpose
issues.problem: MMWR describes KIM D27 as 'attenuated as a result of defects in its ability to acquire iron' and 'widely used by laboratory researchers'. It never says the weakening was done deliberately. pgm-negative strains usually come from a spontaneous deletion that was then selected for, not engineered. The hook makes an unsourced claim.
issues.fix: In 2009, a researcher in Chicago died from a weakened, or attenuated, plague strain that wasn't known to have caused any lab infection before.

issues.problem: Same unsourced 'on purpose' claim, here on screen.
issues.fix: on_screen_text: "Attenuated = weakened". Narration: "To make that work safer, researchers often use attenuated strains: weakened versions of the bacterium. This one was widely used in research and wasn't known to have caused lab infections or human deaths."

issues.claim: His tissues showed iron overload. / Overload found in his tissues
issues.problem: MMWR: 'Histologic staining revealed abnormal iron deposits in the liver, but not in pancreatic or cardiac tissues.' 'Tissues' overgeneralizes. Scene s33's NIH description (liver and heart) could also make viewers think his heart was affected.
issues.fix: Narration: "His liver showed abnormal iron deposits." stat_label: "Abnormal iron deposits in his liver (autopsy)"

issues.claim: CDC's own recommendation is that clinicians ask about work exposures, so the list of possible diagnoses can be widened to include infections picked up at work.
issues.problem: MMWR has two separate statements: 'Unexpected acute illness in a laboratory worker should be reported to the institution and health-care providers so that the differential diagnosis can be expanded…' and 'health-care providers should routinely inquire about occupational exposures'. The script attaches the purpose clause to the wrong recommendation.
issues.fix: And say the thing this 2009 case turned on. Tell them about the possible exposure. CDC's report says health-care providers should routinely ask about work exposures, and that unexpected illness in a lab worker should be reported so the list of possible diagnoses can include infections picked up at work.

issues.claim: Unexpected illness in a laboratory worker should be reported to the institution.
issues.problem: The report says 'to the institution and health-care providers'. Half of the recommendation is dropped.
issues.fix: Unexpected illness in a laboratory worker should be reported to the institution and to health-care providers. And health-care providers should routinely ask patients about their work exposures.

issues.claim: List shows 3 items including 'Tell clinicians your work'
issues.problem: The narration names only 2 items, so the on-screen list doesn't match it.
issues.fix: Narration: "It has to depend on the routine. Protective equipment used every time, illness reported early, and clinicians told about your work."

issues.claim: And many people have no symptoms for years.
issues.problem: The cited NIDDK Definition & Facts page supports 1 in 15 and lower prevalence in people of Asian or African ancestry. It says symptoms usually appear after age 40 but doesn't state 'no symptoms for years' outright.
issues.fix: Replace with: "And symptoms usually don't appear until after age 40, according to NIH."

issues.claim: BMBL recommends BSL-2 for clinical materials and cultures of Y. pestis; BSL-3 for high droplet/aerosol potential
issues.problem: The wording matches the BMBL Y. pestis agent summary, but the cited URL is the BMBL landing page, which doesn't contain that text.
issues.fix: Keep the landing page in the source list but mention 'Agent Summary Statement: Yersinia pestis (BMBL 6th ed., Section VIII-A)' in the description, or link the full BMBL PDF.
